title: Tenth Line
statement:
On LeetCode this is a Bash problem: write a command that outputs line number 10 of the text file `file.txt` and nothing else. The app has no shell, so here you write a JavaScript function `tenthLine(content)`. It receives the whole text of the file and returns exactly what the command would output, without the final line break.

Lines are separated by `\n`. A `\n` at the very end of the text ends the last line; it does not begin a new one. Count lines from 1 and return the 10th one unchanged (it may be empty or contain spaces). If the file has fewer than 10 lines, the command outputs nothing, so return the empty string.

notes:
## Intuition

Number the lines and keep only the one numbered 10. The shell has several tools that number lines for you:

- `sed -n '10p' file.txt`: `-n` turns off sed's habit of printing every line, and the command `10p` prints line 10 alone.
- `awk 'NR == 10' file.txt`: awk keeps the current line number in `NR`; the pattern is true only on line 10, and a pattern without an action prints the line.
- `tail -n +10 file.txt | head -n 1`: `tail -n +10` starts its output at line 10, and `head -n 1` keeps the first line of that.

All three print nothing for a file with fewer than 10 lines. The JavaScript reference does the same with `split`.

## Approach

1. Split `content` at every `\n` into `lines`.
2. If the text ends with `\n`, the split leaves one empty piece after it that is not a real line, so drop it with `pop`.
3. If fewer than 10 lines remain, return `''`: the command would print nothing.
4. Otherwise return `lines[9]`, the 10th line (arrays count from 0).

## Example 1, step by step

`content` is `"Line 1\nLine 2\n…\nLine 10"` with no final line break.

- `split('\n')` gives 10 pieces, `"Line 1"` to `"Line 10"`.
- The text does not end with `\n`, so nothing is dropped.
- `lines.length` is 10, not below 10.
- The function returns `lines[9]`, which is `"Line 10"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) for n characters, since `split` reads the text once.
- Space: O(n) for the pieces. sed and awk stream the file instead and hold one line at a time; `sed -n '10{p;q}'` even stops reading after line 10.

## Pitfalls

- `head -n 10 file.txt | tail -n 1` prints the last line of a short file instead of nothing.
- `lines[9]` of an array with fewer than 10 entries is `undefined`, not `''`: check the length first (or write `lines[9] ?? ''`).
- Trimming the line changes the answer: the 10th line comes back exactly as it is, spaces and tabs included.
- Off by one: the 10th line is `lines[9]`, not `lines[10]`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `content` | the whole text of `file.txt` |
| `lines` | the pieces of `content` between line breaks, one per line |

narration.1: tenthLine receives the whole file as one string and returns what the command would print.
narration.2: Cut the text at every line break; each piece is one line.
narration.3: A line break at the very end leaves an empty piece after it, which is not a real line.
narration.4: Drop that empty piece so the count matches what sed or awk would see.
narration.6: A file shorter than 10 lines has no 10th line.
narration.7: The command prints nothing in that case, so return the empty string.
narration.9: Otherwise the 10th line sits at index 9.
